title: Coping in motion: An ecological momentary assessment study examining the dynamic interplay of leisure‐time physical activity, self‐efficacy and perceived stress
abstract: Abstract Objectives This study examined the associations between leisure‐time physical activity (LTPA), LTPA‐specific self‐efficacy and perceived stress, based on the transactional model of stress and coping. While the health benefits of LTPA are well established, less is known about the potential coping functions of LTPA and how LTPA‐specific self‐efficacy may operate as a personal resource related to daily stress. Given the dynamic nature of stress, coping processes and personal resources, the analyses focused on both within‐person associations and between‐person differences. Design This study is a secondary analysis of a larger longitudinal observational study including n = 256 participants (age: M = 41.93; SD = 12.27; 57% female) who took part in a 14‐day Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA). Methods Five times daily, participants reported LTPA during the preceding 2.5 h, self‐efficacy and stress via a smartphone app. Multilevel modelling was used to examine within‐ and between‐person associations between LTPA, LTPA‐specific self‐efficacy and perceived stress, adjusting for demographic and work‐related covariates, low back pain and time trends. Results Participants completed on average 82% of measurements. At the within‐person level, both concurrent and lagged LTPA, as well as concurrent LTPA‐specific self‐efficacy, were associated with lower momentary stress. At the between‐person level, higher average LTPA‐specific self‐efficacy was associated with lower perceived stress. Conclusions EMA findings suggest that LTPA may serve coping functions, while LTPA‐specific self‐efficacy may represent a personal resource for daily stress regulation. These findings could inform future intervention research—including just‐in‐time adaptive approaches—that target LTPA and self‐efficacy in daily life.
